 AP-75 Barriers to affordable housing – 91.220(j)

Introduction

A barrier to affordable housing is a public policy or nongovernmental condition that constrains the
development or rehabilitation of affordable housing, such as land use controls, property taxes, state prevailing
wage requirements, environmental protection, cost of land and availability of monetary resources. Barriers
to affordable housing are distinguished from impediments to fair housing choice in the sense that barriers are
lawful and impediments to fair housing choice are usually unlawful.

Based on information gathered during community meetings, the Consolidated Plan survey, the 2013-2021
Housing Element and market analysis, the primary barriers to affordable housing in Palmdale are housing
affordability and the lack of monetary resources necessary to develop and sustain affordable housing. The
two barriers are related in the sense that demand for affordable housing exceeds the supply and insufficient
resources are available to increase the supply of affordable housing to meet demand.

Actions it planned to remove or ameliorate the negative effects of public policies that serve as barriers to
affordable housing such as land use controls, tax policies affecting land, zoning ordinances, building codes,
fees and charges, growth limitations, and policies affecting the return on residential investment

In the development of the 2013-2021 Housing Element, the City evaluated significant public policies affecting
affordable housing development such as land use controls, tax policies affecting land, zoning ordinances,
building codes, fees and charges and growth limitations. Based on this evaluation, the City determined that
it has taken all necessary steps to ameliorate the negative effects of public policies that may have been a
barrier to affordable housing. Moreover, the City is actively engaged with affordable housing developers
concerning the siting of affordable housing and ensuring that the entitlement process runs smoothly from
inception to completion.

City of Palmdale  - 49 -  2021 Annual Action Plan
 AP-85 Other Actions – 91.220(k)

Introduction

In the implementation of the 2021-2022 Annual Action Plan, the City will invest CDBG and HOME resources
to address obstacles to meet underserved needs, foster and maintain affordable housing, reduce lead-based
paint hazards, reduce the number of poverty-level families, develop institutional structure and enhance
coordination between public and private housing and social service agencies.

Actions planned to address obstacles to meeting underserved needs

The primary obstacles to meeting the underserved needs of low- and moderate-income people include lack
of funding from federal, state and other local sources, the high cost of housing that is not affordable to low-
income people and the lack of availability of home improvement financing in the private lending industry. To
address these obstacles, the City is investing CDBG and HOME funds through the 2021-2022 Annual Action
Plan in projects that will provide public services to low- and moderate-income people to prevent
homelessness, rental assistance to low-income households, and projects that provide the infrastructure
necessary to facilitate access to public facilities where services are provided. To address underserved needs,
the City is allocating the majority of its CDBG and HOME funds (excluding Section 108 Debt Service and
Administration) for program year 2021-2022 to projects that benefit low- and moderate-income people.

Actions planned to foster and maintain affordable housing

In the implementation of the 2021-2022 Annual Action Plan, the City will invest HOME funds to foster
affordable housing by partnering with housing developers in an effort to support the development of new
rental housing units, and provide tenant-based rental assistance to low-income tenants requiring affordable
housing..

Actions planned to reduce lead-based paint hazards

The Residential Lead Based Paint Hazard Reduction Act of 1992 (Title X) emphasizes prevention of childhood
lead poisoning through housing-based approaches. To reduce lead-based paint hazards, the City of
Palmdale will conduct lead-based paint testing and risk assessments for future rehabilitation projects where
the property to be assisted was built prior to January 1, 1978 and will incorporate safe work practices or
abatement into the scope of work as required to reduce lead-based paint hazards in accordance with 24
CFR Part 35.

City of Palmdale  - 50 -  2021 Annual Action Plan
 Actions planned to reduce the number of poverty-level families

The implementation of CDBG and HOME activities meeting the goals established in the 2020-2024
Consolidated Plan - Strategic Plan and this Annual Action Plan will help to reduce the number of poverty-
level families by:

  •  Supporting activities that increase the supply of housing that is affordable to low- and moderate-
  income households;
  •  Supporting activities that ensure equal access to housing opportunities;
  •  Supporting public service activities that address homelessness and special needs populations;
  •  Supporting activities that improve public facilities and infrastructure; and
  •  Supporting economic opportunity programs to help families recover from the economic impacts of
  the COVID-19 pandemic that began in early 2020.

In addition to these local efforts, mainstream state and federal resources also contribute to reducing the
number of individuals and families in poverty. Federal programs such as the Earned Income Tax Credit and
Head Start provide pathways out of poverty for families who are ready to pursue employment and educational
opportunities. Additionally in California, the primary programs that assist families in poverty are CalWORKS,
CalFresh (formerly food stamps) and Medi-Cal. Together, these programs provide individuals and families
with employment assistance, subsidy for food, medical care, childcare and cash payments to meet basic
needs such as housing, nutrition and transportation. Other services are available to assist persons suffering
from substance abuse, domestic violence and mental illness.

Actions planned to develop institutional structure

To address the lack of resources necessary to support local programs in Palmdale for special needs
populations and persons experiencing homelessness, the City’s Departments continue to facilitate strategic
regional partnerships in L.A. County to bring resources into the Antelope Valley. The City’s partnership
between SAVES and the Los Angeles Regional Foodbank, forged during the previous planning cycle, is an
example of the level of determination the City has to provide essential services to its residents. The
Department of Administrative Services continues to search for alternate funding sources.

Actions planned to enhance coordination between public and private housing and social service agencies

To enhance coordination between public and private housing and social service agencies, the City will
continue consulting with and inviting the participation of a wide variety of agencies and organizations involved
in the delivery of housing and supportive services to low- and moderate-income residents in Palmdale—
particularly the low-and moderate- income areas.

Title 16 – “Subdivisions" of the City’s Municipal Code was last updated was in 1996. Title

control the division of land within the City of Palmdale and to supplement the provisions
of the State’s Subdivision Map Act concerning the design, improvement and survey data
of subdivisions, the form and content of all required maps, and the procedure to be
followed in securing the City’s official approval of all required maps. There have been a
number of changes to the State Subdivision Map Act and City policies and procedures
since the last update of these provisions in 1996.

DISCUSSION
The City’s Public Works Department staff enlisted the services of a consultant to assist in
the (1) analysis of the code; (2) development of revised code language incorporating
changes and updates to subdivision regulations, and (3) preparation of a City specific
guide for the development community entitled “Guide for the Preparation of Final Maps
and Parcel Maps” and accompanying forms. The guide will assist the applicant
surveyor/engineer in preparing a Final Subdivision Map through the City of Palmdale
Public Works Engineering Division, to provide uniformity, and to streamline the current
procedures. The general practices, policies, and procedures apply to all subdivision maps
processed by the City.

ISSUE
Adopt resolution No. CC 2021-054, authorizing the issuance of City of Palmdale
Community Facilities District No. 05-01 (Trade and Commerce Center Area) 2021
Special Tax Refunding Bonds, and approving related documents and actions.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council, acting as the legislative body of Community
Facilities District No. 05-01 (Trade and Commerce Center Area), adopt Resolution No.
CC 2021-054 authorizing the issuance of City of Palmdale Community Facilities District
No. 05-01 (Trade and Commerce Center Area) 2021 Special Tax Refunding Bonds, and
approving related documents and actions.

BACKGROUND
The City formed Community Facilities District No. 05-1 (Trade and Commerce Center
Area) (“CFD”) in 2005. The CFD encompasses 120 acres bordering Trade and
Commerce Center Drive between Avenue P-4 and Avenue Q. The CFD was formed for
the purpose of issuing special tax bonds to refinance assessment districts and a
community facilities district with liens on the properties within the CFD and for curing
delinquent taxes. There are 3 series of CFD Special Tax Bonds outstanding:

 2005 Series A  $ 4,160,000  6.25%
 Converted 2005 Series A  1,080,000  6.75%
 2007 Series A  5,145,000  6.125%
  $10,385,000

The City had issued a subordinate 2005 Series B Bond for the CFD, which was converted
to a parity 2005 Series A Bond in 2011 (referred to as the Converted 2005 Series A Bond)
when it achieved the ratios necessary for conversion.

All of the parcels of taxable property in the CFD are finished lots, with all off-site
improvements completed (including curbs, gutters, sidewalks, streetlights and all public
utilities in the streets). Not all taxable property in the CFD has been developed.
Approximately 69% of the special tax applicable to the 2005 Bonds is levied on
undeveloped property and approximately 94% of the special tax applicable to the 2007
Bonds is levied on undeveloped property. Three of the undeveloped parcels are currently
owned by the Successor Agency.

DISCUSSION
On May 6, 2021, the Council was presented with an opportunity to refinance the 2005
Series A Bonds, the Converted 2005 Series A Bonds and the 2007 Series A Bonds
(collectively the “Existing Bonds”) at an average estimated interest rate of approximately
4%. A refinancing at this rate produces a total estimated $2.9 million reduction in debt
service payments over 16 years, or approximately $188,000 per year.

These savings will reduce the special tax levy on the properties in the CFD by 17% each
year. This reduction in special tax may make development of the vacant properties more
cost effective - as well as assist the Successor Agency in closing escrow on the properties
in the CFD that are under contract and assist in marketing the other Successor Agency-
owned properties.

The City’s proposed method of refinancing the Existing Bonds is through the issuance of
Special Tax Refunding Bonds (“Refunding Bonds”) to be purchased directly by an
investor. Because of the percentage of undeveloped land remaining in the CFD, and
some recent delinquencies by certain property owners, staff and the municipal advisor
determined that a public sale of bonds would not be the most effective method of
refinancing the Existing Bonds. Rather, the refinancing would be accomplished by finding
one investor to purchase the Refunding Bonds. This financing mechanism is called a
“private placement.” The City used this same process to refinance certain debt in 2014
secured by park assessments, acquisition and retrofit of the street lights in 2017 and
acquisition the records storage facility in 2018.

On May 6, 2021, the City Council was presented with an offer from Western Alliance Bank
(“Bank”) to purchase the Refunding Bonds. The terms of the Bank’s offer (“Commitment
Letter”) include an interest rate based on spread of 3.0% to 77% of the sum of the 8-Year
ICE Interest Rate Swap Rate. Based on current market conditions, the interest rate would
be 3.36% as of May 6, 2021. The City Council authorized the City Manager to accept
the Bank’s offer and execute the Commitment Letter at a date no more than 30 days’ prior
to the expected closing date of the Refunding Bonds and lock in the interest rate.

Final approval of the financing requires that the City Council, acting as the legislative body
of the CFD, adopt a resolution authorizing the Refunding Bonds and the execution of
various documents in connection with the refinancing by the City Manager and Finance
Manager/City Treasurer.

The City Council resolution establishes the following parameters for the Refunding Bonds:
(1) the par amount of the Refunding Bonds cannot exceed $11,000,000, (2) the true
interest cost cannot exceed 4% and (3) the requirements of the Mello-Roos Act are met.

The City Council resolution also approves the form of the following documents:
    A Bond Purchase Agreement between the Bank and the City;
    A Fiscal Agent Agreement between City and US Bank, as fiscal agent; and
    An Escrow Agreement between the City and US Bank, as trustee for the Existing
  Bonds; and

FISCAL IMPACT
There is no fiscal impact to the City. The Refunding Bonds will be payable from special
taxes levied on property within the CFD. The special taxes include all the costs to
administer the CFD. All financing costs associated with the Refunding Bonds are
contingent on the closing of the Refunding Bonds.

STRATEGIC PLAN
Goal II: Ensure long-term fiscal health of the City and maintain funding for services.
  A. Manage resources, costs and liabilities to ensure the City’s long-term fiscal
  health.
  D. Pursue alternative financing opportunities for continued infrastructure

  ARTICLE V

  OTHER COVENANTS OF THE CITY

  Section 5.01. Punctual Payment. The City will punctually pay or cause to be paid the
principal of, and interest and any premium on, the 2021 Bonds when and as due in strict
conformity with the terms of this Agreement and any Supplemental Agreement, and it will
faithfully observe and perform all of the conditions covenants and requirements of this
Agreement and all Supplemental Agreements and of the 2021 Bonds.

  Section 5.02. Limited Obligation. The 2021 Bonds are limited obligations of the City on
behalf of the District and are payable solely from and secured solely by the Special Tax
Revenues and the amounts in the Bond Fund (including the Special Tax Prepayments Account
therein), the Reserve Fund and the Special Tax Fund created hereunder.

  Section 5.03. Extension of Time for Payment. In order to prevent any accumulation of
claims for interest after maturity, the City shall not, directly or indirectly, extend or consent to
the extension of the time for the payment of any claim for interest on any of the 2021 Bonds and
shall not, directly or indirectly, be a party to the approval of any such arrangement by
purchasing or funding said claims for interest or in any other manner. In case any such claim
for interest shall be extended or funded, whether or not with the consent of the City, such claim
for interest so extended or funded shall not be entitled, in case of default hereunder, to the
benefits of this Agreement, except subject to the prior payment in full of the principal of all of
the 2021 Bonds then Outstanding and of all claims for interest which shall not have so extended
or funded.

  Section 5.04. Against Encumbrances. The City will not encumber, pledge or place any
charge or lien upon any of the Special Tax Revenues or other amounts pledged to the 2021
Bonds superior to or on a parity with the pledge and lien herein created for the benefit of the
2021 Bonds, except as permitted by this Agreement.

  Section 5.05. Books and Records. The City will keep, or cause to be kept, proper books
of record and accounts, separate from all other records and accounts of the City, in which
complete and correct entries shall be made of all transactions relating to the expenditure of
amounts disbursed from the Administrative Expense Fund and the Special Tax Fund and to the
Special Tax Revenues. Such books of record and accounts shall at all times during business
hours be subject to the inspection of the Fiscal Agent (who shall have no duty to inspect the
same) and the Owners of not less than ten percent (10%) of the principal amount of the 2021
Bonds then Outstanding, or their representatives duly authorized in writing.

  Section 5.06. Protection of Security and Rights of Owners. The City will preserve and
protect the security of the 2021 Bonds and the rights of the Owners, and will warrant and
defend their rights against all claims and demands of all persons. From and after the delivery
of any of the 2021 Bonds by the City, the 2021 Bonds shall be incontestable by the City.

  Section 5.07. Compliance with Law. The City will comply with all applicable provisions
of the Act and law in administering the District.

requirements of the Act so as to assure the timely collection of Special Tax Revenues, including
without limitation, the enforcement of delinquent Special Taxes.

  On or about June 1 of each year, the Fiscal Agent shall provide the Finance Director with
a notice stating the amount then on deposit in the Bond Fund and the Reserve Fund, and
informing the City that the Special Taxes need to be levied pursuant to the Ordinance as

Auditor to ascertain the relevant parcels on which the Special Taxes are to be levied, taking into
account any parcel splits during the preceding and then current year.

accordance with the Ordinance by each July 15 that the 2021 Bonds are outstanding, or

of the amounts of the levy, the Finance Director shall prepare or cause to be prepared, and shall
transmit to the Auditor, such data as the Auditor requires to include the levy of the Special

Director shall make note of any investment of funds hereunder in excess of the yield on the 2021
Bonds, so that appropriate actions can be taken to assure compliance with Section 5.13.

the Finance Director shall be invested by the Finance Director in any Permitted Investment,
which in any event by their terms mature prior to the date on which such moneys are required
to be paid out hereunder. Obligations purchased as an investment of moneys in any fund shall
be deemed to be part of such fund or account, subject, however, to the requirements of this
Agreement for transfer of interest earnings and profits resulting from investment of amounts in
funds and accounts. Whenever in this Agreement any moneys are required to be transferred by

ISSUE
Adopt Resolution CC 2021-044, proposing to establish the Palmdale Enhanced
Infrastructure Financing District (EIFD) and establish a Public Financing Authority
(PFA).

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Adopt Resolution CC 2021-044, proposing to establish the Palmdale EIFD;
  2. Establish a PFA and appoint members; and,
  3. Authorize the City Manager or his designee to prepare and execute all
  necessary documents.

BACKGROUND
In response to the elimination of redevelopment agencies and to support sustainability
goals, the State legislature passed California Senate Bill 628, effective January 1,
2015, and California Assembly Bill 313, effective January 1, 2016, creating an
alternative path to use tax increment financing to fund public improvements, referred
to as EIFD. EIFDs provide an opportunity for agencies to issue bonds for an array of
public projects as well as support economic development efforts in specific areas. Tax
increment financing (Part 1 of Division 2 of Title 5 of the Government Code), which is
the basis for the EIFD, uses the growth in property tax revenues contributed by
participating agencies (city, county, special district) to fund local or regional projects.
EIFDs can fund public capital facilities, infrastructure improvements, maintenance for
projects funded by the EIFD, or other specified projects of communitywide
significance. The property tax increment revenue generated within the district does
not add to existing property taxes or impose new taxes to property owners located in
the district. The increased revenue from tax increment can be leveraged for additional
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Proposed Resolution CC 2021-044
June 1, 2021
Page 2

improvements through the issuance of bonds and/or applied to fund improvements
on a “pay-as-you-go” basis from the date of formation. In addition, EIFD property tax
revenues can be augmented by a variety of local taxes, state, or federal funding
programs (e.g., Cap-and-Trade Program, Proposition 68 Parks & Water Bond Act,
Economic Development Administration grants, etc.).

DISCUSSION

Participating Taxing Entities
Unlike Redevelopment, other affected taxing entities are not required to forgo their
tax increment for the district. Each taxing entity that chooses to join an EIFD has the
option to allocate up to 100% of its portion of tax increment to the District. The County
of Los Angeles is a potential tax sharing entity, and the Resolution of Intent provides
the ability for the County to join the EIFD. In January 2021, the City submitted an
application to the County requesting participation in the EIFD. The application was
reviewed by City staff and presented to the LA County Economic Development Policy
Committee in March 2021. The LA County Board of Supervisors may consider
approving a Resolution of Intent to partner with the City on the Palmdale EIFD in June
2021.

The City has met with the County of Los Angeles who is interested in partnering on
the Palmdale EIFD as a taxing entity. The proposed partnership would include the
County contributing a portion of future property tax increment to fund infrastructure
projects in the Antelope Valley. LA County Public Works has provided a draft list of
infrastructure projects that the County wants to include as part of the Palmdale EIFD.
A complete list of infrastructure projects will be identified in the future Infrastructure
Financing Plan (IFP) that will be approved by the PFA.

Resolution of Intent
The Resolution of Intent proposing the establishment of the Palmdale EIFD describes
the following:

    The boundaries of the proposed Palmdale EIFD district planning area include
  22,971 acres, including 4,140 acres located in unincorporated Los Angeles
  County (EXHIBIT A of RESOLUTION CC 2021-044). The areas included in the
  proposed district are primarily undeveloped and lack necessary infrastructure
  needed for development.

    The types of public facilities and development proposed to be financed by the
  Palmdale EIFD include approximately $176 million of infrastructure
  investments needed to support business attraction, job creation, local and
  regional transportation, and housing opportunities (EXHIBIT B of
  RESOLUTION CC 2021-044). Additional infrastructure projects highlighted in
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Proposed Resolution CC 2021-044
June 1, 2021
Page 3

  the IFP will be funded based on the amount of tax increment generated by the
  Palmdale EIFD.

    The Palmdale EIFD is necessary to enable and accelerate the development of
  undeveloped and underdeveloped areas in the community. The areas
  identified in the proposed district will remain undeveloped due to the significant
  cost to build infrastructure needed to serve the sites. The Palmdale EIFD will
  prioritize and fund key infrastructure projects that are cost prohibitive due and
  prevent new development from occurring. These infrastructure investments will
  assist the City’s efforts to create jobs, provide housing opportunities, and invest
  in local and regional transportation projects

    All City property tax increment revenue generated within the Palmdale EIFD
  boundary, above the base year, may be allocated to the Palmdale EIFD – an
  estimated $606 million of future City property tax increment is proposed to be
  dedicated to the Palmdale EIFD over a 50-year period. The Resolution of Intent
  also provides for the ability for Los Angeles County to join the Palmdale EIFD
  at a later date, although Los Angeles County contributing property tax
  increment in the future is at the discretion of the County Board of Supervisors.

Public Financing Authority
Under EIFD law, the EIFD PFA is the governing board of the Palmdale EIFD. Initially
and pursuant to EIFD law, the PFA’s membership is proposed to include three City
Councilmembers, and two public members whose appointment will be approved by
City Council at a future meeting.

Once the PFA is formed and the members are appointed, the PFA will review and
facilitate public hearings on the IFP for the Palmdale EIFD. The Plan will include tax
increment revenue projection updates, infrastructure to be financed with Palmdale
EIFD funds, caps to the maximum tax increment revenue and bond authorization, and
district formation and election cost information. The PFA is ultimately responsible for
final adoption of an IFP for the Palmdale EIFD. Prior to final approval of an IFP by the
PFA, the City Council will have an opportunity to review and approve the Plan. City
Council approval of the IFP is required under the EIFD law for allocation of City
property tax revenues to the Palmdale EIFD.

If the County agrees to participate in the Palmdale EIFD, then the PFA membership
shall comprise of two members of the City Council, a public member selected by the
Council, one member of the County Board of Supervisors, and a member of the public
selected by the County. Members shall serve at the pleasure of their respective
appointing legislative bodies.

Public Outreach
There are several steps in the EIFD formation process that require public outreach
and participation. Under the EIFD law, the City Council must direct the City Clerk to
mail a copy of the Resolution of Intent to each landowner within the Palmdale EIFD,
each affected taxing entity, and the PFA. This will constitute the first public outreach.
Subsequent mailings will include the draft IFP and related CEQA documentation and
Notice of Public Hearing. Stakeholders will have the opportunity to voice their opinion
to the PFA at the Public Hearing. Additionally, any issuance of bonds by the Palmdale
EIFD in the future will involve public outreach.

Next Steps
The following are the key next steps involved in forming the proposed Palmdale EIFD:

    City Council adoption of Resolution of Intent to form EIFD, creating the EIFD
  PFA;

    City draft the IFP;

    Draft IFP distributed to property owners and affected taxing entities;

    PFA conducts three public hearings to approve IFP and form EIFD; and,

    Filing with Board of Equalization (BOE) per guidelines from Board for Change
  of Jurisdictional Boundaries.

Establishing the Palmdale EIFD will attract new private investment and accelerate
development in key areas of the city, helping create new jobs, housing opportunities and
local and regional transportation options for the region. The Palmdale EIFD creates a
new revenue source to fund necessary infrastructure projects that helps accelerate $3.7
billion in potential new development and will create an estimated 39,000 (7,000
permanent) new jobs for the region. The areas being included in the Palmdale EIFD are
largely undeveloped and currently lack infrastructure needed to attract new development
projects.

The City has collaborated with the County of Los Angeles to establish the Palmdale
EIFD. The partnership with the County will create additional revenue for the Palmdale
EIFD and support the long-term development of unincorporated areas of Los Angeles
County. Some of the infrastructure projects identified in the IFP will directly support
existing employers at U.S. Air Force Plant 42 and support future development adjacent
to Plant 42.

FISCAL IMPACT
The City’s consultant conducted a baseline tax increment analysis to determine the
Palmdale EIFD revenue potential based on estimated future development potential.
Actual tax increment revenues are subject to changes in the types and timing of
development and the real estate market. Based on a total new development value of
approximately $3.7 Billion, if the City contributes 100% of its share of property tax
increment (average 17.5 cents on the dollar) within the Palmdale EIFD, revenues will total
$606 million over 50 years.

While the Palmdale EIFD would benefit from a new dedicated revenue source for
infrastructure improvements, formation of the Palmdale EIFD results in a reallocation of
incremental property tax revenue from the City’s General Fund. Once the Palmdale EIFD
terminates in 50 years, incremental property tax revenue would no longer be allocated to
the Palmdale EIFD and will flow back into the City’s General Fund. The aforementioned
tax increment projections are based upon various assumptions made utilizing the future
growth potential of the residential, commercial, and industrial development sectors in the
area.

  Description of Facilities

The Palmdale EIFD will finance the purchase, construction, expansion, improvement,
seismic retrofit, or rehabilitation of any real or other tangible property with an estimated
useful life of 15 years or longer and are projects of communitywide significance that
provide significant benefits to the district or the surrounding community. The Palmdale
EIFD may also finance the ongoing or capitalized costs to maintain public capital facilities
financed in whole or in part by the Palmdale EIFD. Any facilities located outside the
boundaries of the Palmdale EIFD shall also have a tangible connection to the work of the
Palmdale EIFD as detailed in the infrastructure financing plan. The Palmdale EIFD will
also finance planning and design activities that are directly related to the purchase,
construction, expansion, or rehabilitation of these projects. The Palmdale EIFD may
finance costs described in Government code sections 53398.52, 53398.56 and 53398.57.
Projects financed by the Palmdale EIFD may include, but not limited to, all the following:

  •  Highways, interchanges, ramps and bridges, arterial streets, parking facilities,
  bicycle lanes, and transit facilities;
  •  Parks, recreational facilities, and open space;
  •  Sewage treatment and water reclamation plants and infrastructure;
  •  Facilities for the collection and treatment of water for urban uses;
  •  Facilities for the transfer and disposal of solid waste;
  •  Storm water conveyance and collection facilities;
  •  Flood control, retention basins, detention basins, and drainage channels;
  •  Broadband and telecommunications infrastructure;
  •  Sidewalks and streetscape improvements including pedestrian paths;
  •  Public art
  •  Fire and Police facilities;
  •  Brownfield restoration and other environmental mitigation;
  •  Affordable housing as authorized under the EIFD Law
  •  Projects that implement a sustainable communities strategy; and
  •  Acquisition, construction, or repair of industrial structures for private use.

Other Expenses

In addition to the direct costs of the above facilities, other incidental expenses as
authorized by the EIFD Law, including, but not limited to, the cost of environmental
evaluation and environmental remediation; engineering and surveying; construction
staking; utility relocation and demolition costs incidental to the construction of the
facilities; costs of project/construction management; costs (including the costs of legal
services) associated with the creation of the EIFD; issuance of bonds or other debt; costs
incurred by the County or the EIFD in connection with the division of taxes pursuant to
Government Code section 53398.75; or costs otherwise incurred in order to carry out the
authorized purposes of the EIFD; reimbursements to other areas for facilities serving the
EIFD; and any other expenses incidental to the formation and implementation of the EIFD
and to the construction, completion, inspection and acquisition of the authorized facilities.
